{{Short description|Weak form of the axiom of choice}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''axiom of dependent choice''', denoted by <math> \mathsf{DC} </math>, is a weak form of the [[axiom of choice]] (<math> \mathsf{AC} </math>) that is still sufficient to develop much of [[real analysis]]. It was introduced by [[Paul Bernays]] in a 1942 article in [[reverse mathematics]] that explores which [[set-theoretic]] [[axiom]]s are needed to develop analysis.<ref group=lower-alpha>"The foundation of analysis does not require the full generality of set theory but can be accomplished within a more restricted frame." {{cite journal |last=Bernays |first=Paul |year=1942 |title=Part&nbsp;III. Infinity and enumerability. Analysis. |journal=[[Journal of Symbolic Logic]] |series=A system of axiomatic set theory |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=65–89 |mr=0006333 |doi=10.2307/2266303 |jstor=2266303 |s2cid=250344853 |url=http://doc.rero.ch/record/290936/files/S0022481200064185.pdf}} The axiom of dependent choice is stated on p.&nbsp;86.</ref>

== Formal statement ==
A [[homogeneous relation]] <math>R</math> on <math>X</math> is called a [[total relation]] if for every <math>a \in X,</math> there exists some <math>b \in X</math> such that <math>a\,R~b</math>.

The axiom of dependent choice can be stated as follows: 
For every nonempty [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>X</math> and every total relation  <math>R</math> on <math>X,</math> there exists a [[sequence]] <math>(x_n)_{n \in \N}</math> in <math>X</math> such that 
:<math>x_n\, R~x_{n + 1}</math> for all <math>n \in \N.</math>

In fact, <math>x_0</math> may be taken to be any desired element of <math>X</math>. (To see this, apply the axiom as stated above to the set of finite sequences that start with <math>x_0</math> and in which subsequent terms are in relation <math>R</math>, together with the total relation on this set of the second sequence being obtained from the first by appending a single term.)

If the set <math>X</math> above is restricted to be the set of all [[real number]]s, then the resulting axiom is denoted by <math>\mathsf{DC}_{\R}. </math>

== Use ==
Even without such an axiom, for any <math>n</math>, one can use ordinary mathematical induction to form the first <math>n</math> terms of such a sequence.
The axiom of dependent choice says that we can form a whole ([[countably infinite]]) sequence this way.

The axiom <math> \mathsf{DC} </math> is the fragment of <math> \mathsf{AC} </math> that is required to show the existence of a sequence constructed by [[transfinite recursion]] of [[Countable set|countable]] length, if it is necessary to make a choice at each step and if some of those choices cannot be made independently of previous choices.

== Equivalent statements ==
Over <math> \mathsf{ZF} </math> ([[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] without the axiom of choice), <math> \mathsf{DC} </math> is equivalent to the [[Baire category theorem]] for complete metric spaces.<ref>"The Baire category theorem implies the principle of dependent choices." {{cite journal |last=Blair |first=Charles E. |year=1977 |title=The Baire category theorem implies the principle of dependent choices |journal=Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. Sér. Sci. Math. Astron. Phys. |volume=25 |issue=10 |pages=933–934}}</ref>

It is also equivalent over <math> \mathsf{ZF} </math> to the [[downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem]].<ref group=lower-alpha>Moore states that "Principle of Dependent Choices <math>\Rightarrow</math> Löwenheim–Skolem theorem" — that is, <math>\mathsf{DC}</math> implies the Löwenheim–Skolem theorem. ''See'' table {{cite book |last=Moore |first=Gregory H. |year=1982 |title=Zermelo's Axiom of Choice: Its origins, development, and influence |publisher=Springer |isbn=0-387-90670-3 |page=325}}</ref><ref>The [[Converse (logic)|converse]] is proved in {{cite book |last1=Boolos |first1=George S. |author1link=George Boolos |last2=Jeffrey |first2=Richard C. |author2link=Richard Jeffrey |year=1989 |title=Computability and Logic |edition=3rd |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-38026-X |pages=[https://archive.org/details/computabilitylog0000bool_c7g3/page/155 155–156] |url=https://archive.org/details/computabilitylog0000bool_c7g3/page/155 |url-access=registration}}</ref>

<math> \mathsf{DC} </math> is also equivalent over <math> \mathsf{ZF} </math> to the statement that every [[pruned tree]] with <math> \omega </math> levels has a [[Branch (descriptive set theory)|branch]] (''proof below'').

Furthermore, <math> \mathsf{DC} </math> is equivalent to a weakened form of [[Zorn's lemma]]; specifically <math> \mathsf{DC} </math> is equivalent to the statement that any [[partial order]] such that every [[well-ordered]] [[Chain (ordered set)|chain]] is finite and bounded, must have a maximal element.<ref name="Wolk 1983">{{citation |last=Wolk |first=Elliot S. |year=1983 |title=On the principle of dependent choices and some forms of Zorn's lemma |journal=[[Canadian Mathematical Bulletin]] |doi=10.4153/CMB-1983-062-5 |doi-access=free |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=365–367}}</ref>

{| class="wikitable collapsible collapsed"
! style="background: #f5f5f5;" |Proof that <math>\,\mathsf{DC} \iff</math> Every pruned tree with ω levels has a branch
|- style="text-align: left; vertical-align: top; style="background: white" 
|<math>(\,\Longleftarrow\,)</math> Let <math>R</math> be an entire binary relation on <math>X</math>. The strategy is to define a tree <math>T</math> on <math>X</math> of finite sequences whose neighboring elements satisfy <math>R.</math> Then a branch through <math>T</math> is an infinite sequence whose neighboring elements satisfy <math>R.</math> Start by defining <math>\langle x_0, \dots, x_n\rangle \in T</math> if <math>x_k R\,x_{k+1}</math> for <math>0 \le k < n.</math> Since <math>R</math> is entire, <math>T</math> is a pruned tree with <math>\omega</math> levels. Thus, <math>T</math> has a branch <math>\langle x_0, \dots, x_n, \dots\rangle.</math> So, for all <math>n \ge 0\!:</math> <math>\langle x_0, \dots, x_n, x_{n+1}\rangle \in T,</math> which implies <math>x_nR\,x_{n+1}.</math> Therefore, <math>\mathsf{DC}</math> is true.

<math>(\,\Longrightarrow\,)</math> Let <math>T</math> be a pruned tree on <math>X</math> with <math>\omega</math> levels. The strategy is to define a binary relation <math>R</math> on <math>T</math> so that <math>\mathsf{DC}</math> produces a sequence <math>t_n = \langle x_0, \dots, x_{f(n)} \rangle</math> where <math>t_nR\,t_{n+1}</math> and <math>f(n)</math> is a [[strictly increasing]] function. Then the infinite sequence <math>\langle x_0, \dots, x_k, \dots \rangle</math> is a branch. (This proof only needs to prove this for <math>f(n) = m + n.</math>) Start by defining <math>u\,R\,v</math> if <math>u</math> is an initial subsequence of <math>v,\operatorname{length}(u) > 0,\,</math> and <math>\operatorname{length}(v) =</math> <math>\operatorname{length}(u) + 1.</math> Since <math>T</math> is a pruned tree with <math>\omega</math> levels, <math>R</math> is entire. Therefore, <math>\mathsf{DC}</math> implies that there is an infinite sequence <math>t_n</math> such that <math>t_n\,R\,t_{n+1}.</math> Now <math>t_0 = \langle x_0, \dots, x_m \rangle</math> for some <math>m \ge 0.</math> Let <math>x_{m+n}</math> be the last element of <math>t_n.</math> Then <math>t_n = \langle x_0, \dots, x_m, \dots, x_{m+n} \rangle.</math> For all <math>k \ge 0,</math> the sequence <math>\langle x_0, \dots, x_k \rangle</math> belongs to <math>T</math> because it is an initial subsequence of <math>t_0\, (k \le m)</math> or it is a <math>t_n\, (k \ge m).</math> Therefore, <math>\langle x_0, \dots, x_k, \dots \rangle</math> is a branch.
|}

== Relation with other axioms ==
Unlike full <math> \mathsf{AC} </math>, <math> \mathsf{DC} </math> is insufficient to prove (given <math> \mathsf{ZF} </math>) that there is a [[nonmeasurable|non-measurable]] set of real numbers, or that there is a set of real numbers without the [[property of Baire]] or without the [[perfect set property]]. This follows because the [[Solovay model]] satisfies <math> \mathsf{ZF} + \mathsf{DC} </math>, and every set of real numbers in this model is [[Lebesgue measurable]], has the Baire property and has the perfect set property.

The axiom of dependent choice implies the [[axiom of countable choice]] and is strictly stronger.<ref>Bernays proved that the axiom of dependent choice implies the axiom of countable choice ''See esp.'' p.&nbsp;86 in {{cite journal |last=Bernays |first=Paul |year=1942 |title=Part&nbsp;III. Infinity and enumerability. Analysis. |journal=Journal of Symbolic Logic |series=A system of axiomatic set theory |mr=0006333 |doi=10.2307/2266303 |jstor=2266303 |s2cid=250344853 |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=65–89 |url=http://doc.rero.ch/record/290936/files/S0022481200064185.pdf}}</ref><ref>For a proof that the Axiom of Countable Choice does not imply the Axiom of Dependent Choice ''see'' {{Citation |last=Jech |first=Thomas |authorlink=Thomas Jech |year=1973 |title=The Axiom of Choice |publisher=North Holland |isbn=978-0-486-46624-8 |pages=130–131}}</ref>

It is possible to generalize the axiom to produce transfinite sequences. If these are allowed to be arbitrarily long, then it becomes equivalent to the full axiom of choice.
